purpose: Structured research for overlooked large-memory AI accelerators relevant to local or on-premises LLM inference. Platform-only, region-restricted, and vendor-runtime-specific constraints are preserved explicitly; theoretical compute and memory figures are not presented as normalized token-generation benchmarks.

interconnect: 128 GB/s peak per-link bandwidth as specified by AMD
hardware.form_factor: OCP Accelerator Module (OAM), normally deployed on an 8-GPU UBB 2.0 platform
hardware.cooling: passive OAM; requires qualified server/platform airflow and thermal design
software: TensorFlow ecosystem via ROCm where supported
hardware.quantization_compatibility: ROCm/vLLM supports modern low-precision inference paths including FP8 on MI300X. GGUF/llama.cpp support depends on the exact ROCm/HIP backend and version; do not assume CUDA-specific GPTQ/AWQ kernels are portable without verification.

llm_suitability.practical_guidance: 192GB HBM3 allows many 70B-class models at high precision or with large KV caches on one accelerator and materially reduces model sharding pressure. AMD documents a 66B OPT transformer running on one MI300X. Larger or MoE workloads remain runtime- and context-dependent.

hardware.performance_per_watt_notes: 5.3 TB/s divided by AMD's 750W peak board power is approximately 7.07 GB/s/W. This is a specification-derived memory-bandwidth ratio, not measured LLM efficiency.
physical_constraints: Not a conventional desktop PCIe add-in card; requires an OAM/UBB-compatible server platform.
Passive cooling and 54V platform power require qualified datacenter infrastructure.
AMD's MI300X platform typically integrates eight OAM accelerators; acquiring a bare OAM without a compatible carrier is not equivalent to acquiring a usable local GPU.

pricing.note: AMD directs buyers to solution partners; no defensible public single-accelerator retail price was found for a deployable MI300X OAM/platform configuration.

hardware.cost_efficiency_notes: Purchase economics cannot be normalized credibly from public retail data because MI300X is sold primarily as integrated OEM/solution-partner infrastructure. Used bare-OAM listings should be treated cautiously because carrier, firmware, power and cooling requirements dominate deployability.
source_caveats: Peak matrix/TOPS figures are theoretical vendor specifications and are not equivalent to application throughput.
The 7.07 GB/s/W figure is derived from peak bandwidth and peak board power, not wall-power measurement.
No numeric price is stored because a complete deployable MI300X solution is partner/platform dependent.

hardware.architecture: Habana Gaudi2, 24 Tensor Processor Cores plus Matrix Multiplication Engine
hardware.host_interface: PCIe 4.0 x16 through OCP Accelerator Module 1.1 platform
hardware.scale_out_networking: 24x integrated 100GbE RoCE v2 ports per accelerator
hardware.software_release_state: Current Gaudi documentation lists Gaudi2 on-prem support with Intel Gaudi Software build 1.24.1-482 and a maintained software stack. The 1.22 support matrix includes PyTorch 2.7, TGI 3.3.2 and a vLLM fork based on v0.9.0.1.
hardware.quantization_compatibility: Current Gaudi vLLM documentation supports FP8 models plus FP8 KV-cache quantization/calibration with Intel Neural Compressor. This is a Gaudi-specific runtime path; arbitrary CUDA kernels or GGUF artifacts should not be assumed to execute directly.

llm_suitability.practical_guidance: 96GB HBM2e materially reduces sharding for large models, and Intel's current vLLM guidance validates Llama 2/3/3.1 families including 70B, Mistral and Mixtral across supported single- and multi-HPU configurations. Exact single-accelerator fit and throughput depend on precision, context and runtime overhead.

hardware.performance_per_watt_notes: 2.45 TB/s divided by 600W TDP is approximately 4.08 GB/s/W. This is a specification-derived memory-bandwidth ratio, not measured application efficiency.
physical_constraints: Not a normal desktop PCIe card; HL-225H is an OAM/mezzanine accelerator intended for qualified Gaudi2 systems/baseboards.
600W accelerator power and integrated high-speed networking require datacenter-class power and cooling.
Software portability is lower than CUDA/ROCm because supported models run through the Gaudi software stack and HPU-specific integrations.

pricing.note: No stable public single-card retail price was found for a deployable HL-225H configuration; practical acquisition is generally through Gaudi2 server/platform channels.

hardware.cost_efficiency_notes: Gaudi2 can be compelling when complete systems appear at discounted enterprise/secondary-market pricing because 96GB HBM2e and current vLLM/PyTorch support remain useful. Bare mezzanine price alone is not a valid deployable-system cost.
source_caveats: Gaudi2's public data sheet is an accelerator/OAM specification, not a complete server wall-power figure.
Model validation in Intel's vLLM documentation spans multiple tensor-parallel configurations; the record does not claim every 70B configuration runs on one HPU.
No numeric retail price is stored because acquisition is platform/OEM dependent.

hardware.form_factor: full-height full-length dual-slot, approximately 4.4 in H x 10.5 in L
hardware.cooling: server/datacenter deployment; verify exact OEM thermal implementation
hardware.quantization_compatibility: Ada-class CUDA software supports common FP8/FP16/INT8 inference paths; GGUF via CUDA llama.cpp and other quantized runtimes is generally feasible, but exact kernel/driver support must be verified for region-specific OEM systems.

llm_suitability.practical_guidance: 48GB dedicated VRAM is suitable for many 30B-class models at moderate precision and selected 70B-class models with aggressive 4-bit-class quantization, subject to context/KV-cache overhead. Its value is constrained by regional availability rather than memory capacity.

hardware.performance_per_watt_notes: 864 GB/s divided by 275W is approximately 3.14 GB/s/W. This is a specification-derived memory-bandwidth ratio, not measured LLM performance-per-watt.
physical_constraints: HPE's current QuickSpecs states its L20 accelerator is sold only in China, Hong Kong and Macau.
Availability outside supported regional/OEM channels may involve import, warranty or support limitations.
Server-class power, chassis clearance and airflow should be verified before treating an L20 as a workstation drop-in.

pricing.note: No defensible current public retail price was stored. HPE documents the L20 accelerator as a China/Hong Kong/Macau-only option in its current accelerator QuickSpecs.

hardware.cost_efficiency_notes: Technically attractive as a 48GB Ada card at 275W, but regional/OEM restrictions make purchase economics highly channel-dependent. It should not be compared with globally retailed workstation GPUs using an unverified import listing.
source_caveats: NVIDIA's current public vGPU documentation confirms L20 as a 48GB physical GPU, while detailed board specifications are exposed through OEM QuickSpecs rather than a normal NVIDIA retail product page.
HPE states its L20 option is restricted to China, Hong Kong and Macau.
The 3.14 GB/s/W figure is a derived specification ratio, not an inference benchmark.
